questions.question: What are constraints in SQL and why are they important?
questions.title: SQL Constraints — Enforcing Data Integrity
questions.direct_answer: Constraints are rules enforced by the database: PRIMARY KEY identifies rows, UNIQUE protects candidate keys, FOREIGN KEY enforces references, NOT NULL requires a value, CHECK rejects false conditions, and DEFAULT supplies a value when omitted. DEFAULT is often grouped with constraints for teaching even though products/catalogs may classify it differently. Constraint semantics, especially NULL and referential actions, need precise handling.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the main constraint types and that they enforce integrity at the DB level.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying only on application validation and skipping DB constraints.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Stress that constraints are the last line of defense — enforced even if app code is buggy.

sections.title: SQL Constraints Protect Data Integrity
sections.content:
Choose referential actions deliberately. ON DELETE CASCADE suits privately owned child rows; RESTRICT/NO ACTION suits relationships that should block deletion. UNIQUE NULL behavior varies by database, so add NOT NULL or database-specific syntax when the business key must always exist.

Name important constraints so violations can be identified and translated into stable application errors. Do not expose raw database messages directly to clients.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Constraints protect data from every writer, not only one application.
PRIMARY KEY is unique and not null; one constraint can span several columns.
FOREIGN KEY can reference a suitable primary or unique candidate key.
CHECK normally allows UNKNOWN, so combine with NOT NULL when presence is required.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: An account table can use PRIMARY KEY(id), UNIQUE(iban), NOT NULL(owner_name), and CHECK(balance >= 0). A transfer table can reference account(id) with a foreign key. Application validation gives fast friendly feedback, but the database constraint closes race conditions and protects scripts or other services.

sections.title: Constraints at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|PRIMARY KEY|~row identity|unique + not null|one per table|often auto-increment
emerald|FOREIGN KEY|~links tables|references a PK|enforces referential integrity|CASCADE options
amber|UNIQUE / NOT NULL|~value rules|UNIQUE = no duplicates|NOT NULL = must have value|
rose|CHECK / DEFAULT|~custom + fallback|CHECK = condition|DEFAULT = fallback value|enforced on write

sections.title: Constraints in a CREATE TABLE
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id        INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,      -- unique identity
  email     VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL UNIQUE,         -- required + no duplicates
  dept_id   INT REFERENCES departments(id),       -- foreign key
  salary    DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (salary > 0),     -- custom rule
  status    VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'          -- fallback value
);

-- this fails the CHECK constraint:
INSERT INTO employees (email, salary) VALUES ('a@x.com', -100); -- rejected
```

*The database rejects the negative salary regardless of what the app sent.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Skipping DB constraints**: trusting app validation alone — a second service or a bug can insert bad data.
- **No NOT NULL on required columns**: lets NULLs slip into mandatory fields.
- **Missing FOREIGN KEY**: orphan rows (a child pointing to a deleted parent).
- **Over-constraining**: overly strict CHECKs that block legitimate edge cases.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

seo.metaTitle: SQL Constraints — Enforcing Data Integrity — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What are constraints in SQL and why are they important? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: An employees table with an id PRIMARY KEY, a UNIQUE email, and a CHECK on salary
speakable_v2.hook: Your app code can have bugs. Constraints are the database's own rulebook, and they reject bad data no matter what.

beats.text: A constraint is a rule you attach to a column or table. The database checks it on every insert and update. If the data breaks the rule, the write gets rejected. So constraints keep your data valid and clean.

Most apps trust their own validation code. But code has bugs, and often more than one service writes to the same table. A constraint is the last line of defense. It guards the data even when the app slips up.

items: PRIMARY KEY marks the row's identity. It's unique and never null.
FOREIGN KEY links a row to a parent table and blocks orphan rows.
UNIQUE blocks duplicate values, though it still allows nulls.
NOT NULL forces a column to always hold a value.
CHECK enforces your own condition, like a price above zero.
DEFAULT fills in a fallback value when you skip the column.

beats.text: Picture an employees table. The id is the PRIMARY KEY. Email is NOT NULL and UNIQUE. Salary has a CHECK that keeps it above zero. Try to insert a negative salary and the database rejects it. Here's the non-obvious part. It blocks that row even when your Java code forgot to check.

items: Trusting only app validation. A second service or a bug can still slip bad data in.
Leaving off NOT NULL on a required column, so nulls sneak in.
Skipping a FOREIGN KEY, which leaves orphan rows behind.
Over-tight CHECK rules that block valid edge cases.

speakable_v2.cap: So constraints push your rules into the database itself. Even buggy app code can't sneak past them.
followup_handoff: What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint?
What happens when you violate a FOREIGN KEY constraint?

questions.question: What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint in SQL?
questions.title: PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE Constraint in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A PRIMARY KEY is the table's chosen row identifier: its columns are unique and not null, and a table has at most one primary-key constraint, which may contain several columns. UNIQUE creates another candidate-key rule and a table can have several. How UNIQUE treats nulls is database-specific: many systems allow several nulls, SQL Server commonly allows one in a single-column unique constraint, and PostgreSQL can request NULLS NOT DISTINCT.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know PK is unique+not-null+one-per-table while UNIQUE allows NULL and can repeat.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking UNIQUE forbids NULLs, or that you can have multiple primary keys.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note PK auto-creates a clustered index in many DBs and is the natural FK target.

sections.title: PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE
sections.content:
Primary and unique constraints are logical integrity rules. Databases normally enforce them with indexes, but index implementation details are not the definition. Foreign keys can target a primary key or another referenced candidate key that has an appropriate unique constraint.

Composite keys apply the rule to the combination. PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, order_id) permits the same order_id in two tenants but not the same pair twice. UNIQUE (tenant_id, external_ref) can protect another business rule independently.

**Example.** employee.id can be the table's primary key, while employee.email has a UNIQUE constraint as another candidate key. A table has one primary-key constraint but can have several unique constraints; NULL treatment for UNIQUE is database-specific.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: PRIMARY KEY identifies rows and implies UNIQUE plus NOT NULL.
One primary-key constraint can be composite.
Several UNIQUE constraints can protect other business keys.
Verify NULL behavior in the target database instead of memorizing one rule.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: An orders table can use id as its primary key and order_number as a unique business key. Both reject duplicate non-null values, but only the primary key is the table's designated identity and cannot contain null. A unique email constraint may allow multiple nulls in PostgreSQL or MySQL, behave differently in SQL Server, or be configured differently in newer PostgreSQL. If null must be disallowed, add NOT NULL explicitly.

sections.title: PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE
sections.content:
blue|PRIMARY KEY|~row identity|unique + NOT NULL|one per table|FK target, clustered index
emerald|UNIQUE|~no duplicates|allows NULL|many per table|e.g. email, username
amber|Shared|~both reject duplicates|both can be composite|both back an index|
rose|Choose|~by role|identifier -> PRIMARY KEY|other no-dup column -> UNIQUE|

sections.title: PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE
sections.content:
| Aspect | PRIMARY KEY | UNIQUE |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicates | not allowed | not allowed |
| NULLs | not allowed | allowed |
| Per table | exactly one | many |
| Role | row identity | extra no-dup rule |
| FK target | yes (typical) | possible |

sections.title: Misusing UNIQUE as the identity
sections.content:
```sql
-- email can be NULL, so it's a poor row identity
CREATE TABLE users (
  email VARCHAR(120) UNIQUE,   -- allows NULL, can't reliably identify a row
  name  VARCHAR(80)
);
```

sections.title: PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for email
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id    INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,  -- unique + not null identity
  email VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL UNIQUE,    -- no duplicates, and required
  name  VARCHAR(80)
);
```

*`id` identifies the row; `email` is unique but is not the identity.*

sections.title: When to Use Which
sections.content:
Use a **PRIMARY KEY** for the column (or columns) that identify a row — typically a surrogate `id`. It's the natural target for foreign keys.

Use a **UNIQUE** constraint for any *other* column that must not contain duplicates but isn't the identity — email, username, phone, SKU. Add `NOT NULL` alongside UNIQUE when the value is also required.

followup_questions: Can a UNIQUE column contain NULL values?

seo.metaTitle: PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE Constraint in SQL — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint in SQL? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: An id PRIMARY KEY plus a UNIQUE email on a users table
speakable_v2.hook: People mix these two up all the time. Both block duplicate values, but only one can act as the row's identity.

beats.text: A PRIMARY KEY is the main identity of a row. It's unique and it's never null, and a table gets just one. A UNIQUE constraint also blocks duplicates. But it allows nulls, and a table can hold many of them.

Reach for a PRIMARY KEY on the column that names the row, usually a surrogate id. That's the natural target for foreign keys. Use UNIQUE for any other column that must stay distinct, like email or username. Add NOT NULL next to UNIQUE when the value is also required.

Say email is UNIQUE but nullable. Two rows can both store null at once, because null never equals null. That's the gotcha. A nullable UNIQUE column makes a shaky identity, so keep the id as your PRIMARY KEY.

speakable_v2.cap: So PRIMARY KEY is the one true identity, and UNIQUE is the extra no-duplicates rule you sprinkle on other columns.
followup_handoff: Can multiple rows have NULL for a UNIQUE column?
What is a composite primary key?

questions.question: What is a FOREIGN KEY constraint and what does CASCADE mean?
questions.title: FOREIGN KEY Constraint and CASCADE in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A FOREIGN KEY requires each non-null child key to match a referenced key in another or the same table. The referenced columns are commonly a primary key but can also be a suitable UNIQUE candidate key. ON DELETE CASCADE deletes referencing rows when the parent row is deleted; ON UPDATE CASCADE updates the child keys when the referenced key changes. Other actions and support vary by database.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand FK referential integrity and ON DELETE/UPDATE CASCADE.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming you can delete a parent row that still has children, or misusing CASCADE.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Compare CASCADE vs SET NULL vs RESTRICT and warn that CASCADE can delete more than expected.

sections.title: FOREIGN KEY and Referential Actions
sections.content:
Foreign-key checks use the database's transaction and locking rules. They protect against orphan references even when a script or another service writes directly. Index the child foreign-key columns when deletes, updates, or joins need it; some databases do not create that child-side index automatically.

Self-references such as employee.manager_id are valid. Composite foreign keys must match the referenced key's column set and compatible types. NULL semantics, deferred checking, update actions, and DDL syntax should be verified for the selected database.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Foreign keys enforce relationships for every writer, not just one application.
A nullable foreign key permits no relationship unless NOT NULL is also declared.
The target can be a primary or qualifying unique key.
Choose CASCADE only when child lifetime or key propagation truly follows the parent.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: order_items.order_id can reference orders.id. Inserting an item with a non-null order_id that has no matching order is rejected. With ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting an order deletes its items. For shared or historically important rows, RESTRICT/NO ACTION or a soft-delete design may be safer. CASCADE does not mean every parent change automatically copies every column; it applies to the specific referenced delete or key-update event.

sections.title: FOREIGN KEY at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~links child to parent|references parent PK|referential integrity|no orphan rows
emerald|ON DELETE CASCADE|~delete children too|parent gone -> children gone|tidy, but powerful|can delete a lot
amber|SET NULL|~keep child, null link|parent gone -> FK = NULL|column must be nullable|
rose|RESTRICT / NO ACTION|~block the delete|parent kept if children exist|safe default|

sections.title: Foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting to delete a parent with children**: blocked unless you set CASCADE/SET NULL.
- **CASCADE deleting too much**: `ON DELETE CASCADE` can wipe large subtrees — use deliberately.
- **SET NULL on a NOT NULL column**: invalid — the FK column must be nullable.
- **Type mismatch**: the FK column must match the referenced PK's type.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

seo.metaTitle: FOREIGN KEY Constraint and CASCADE in SQL — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is a FOREIGN KEY constraint and what does CASCADE mean? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: An orders table whose customer_id is a FOREIGN KEY to customers(id)
speakable_v2.hook: A foreign key won't let an order point to a customer who doesn't exist. But cascade can quietly delete a lot.

beats.text: A foreign key is a column in a child table that points to the primary key of a parent table. It enforces a simple promise. Every child must point to a parent that really exists. So orphan rows that reference nothing simply can't appear.
Without this link, nothing stops a row from pointing at a deleted parent. Reports break and joins return junk. A foreign key keeps the two tables honest, so the relationship stays valid at all times.

items: ON DELETE CASCADE deletes the children when the parent goes.
ON DELETE SET NULL keeps the child but blanks its link. The column has to be nullable.
ON DELETE RESTRICT blocks the delete while children still exist. This is the safe default.
ON UPDATE CASCADE copies a changed parent key down to the children.

beats.text: Picture orders linked to customers with ON DELETE CASCADE. You delete customer five. The database removes that customer and all their orders in one shot. Here's the non-obvious part. One delete at the top can wipe a whole tree of related rows below it.

items: Trying to delete a parent that still has children. The database blocks it unless you set an action.
Reaching for CASCADE everywhere, then losing more rows than you meant to.
SET NULL on a NOT NULL column, which simply can't work.
A foreign key type that doesn't match the parent key type.

speakable_v2.cap: So a foreign key stops orphan rows, and the action you pick decides how deletes ripple down.
followup_handoff: What is the difference between ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE RESTRICT?
Should FOREIGN KEY columns be indexed?

questions.question: What is the CHECK constraint in SQL?
questions.title: CHECK Constraint in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A CHECK constraint requires its condition not to be FALSE. In standard SQL, TRUE and UNKNOWN pass, so CHECK (salary > 0) does not by itself reject NULL salary. Add NOT NULL when a value is required. CHECK is useful for row-level rules such as valid ranges or a known set of statuses; exact feature support and function restrictions vary by database.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know CHECK enforces a custom condition at the DB level.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying only on app validation, or assuming older MySQL enforces CHECK (it ignored it pre-8.0.16).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note CHECK treats UNKNOWN (NULL) as passing, and mention enum-style CHECK with IN.

sections.title: CHECK Constraints and Three-valued Logic
sections.content:
A CHECK protects data regardless of whether it comes from the application, a migration, or an admin query. Give important constraints clear names so an error can be diagnosed.

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE account (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  balance DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT chk_account_status CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE', 'CLOSED')),
  CONSTRAINT chk_balance_nonnegative CHECK (balance >= 0)
);
~~~

Application validation can produce friendlier messages, but it should not replace database integrity rules.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: FALSE violates a CHECK; TRUE passes; UNKNOWN usually passes.
Combine CHECK with NOT NULL when null must be rejected.
Use it for rules the database can evaluate from the row.
Do not assume every database permits subqueries or volatile functions in CHECK expressions.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: CHECK (age >= 18) rejects age 12 but normally accepts NULL because NULL >= 18 is UNKNOWN. Define age INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (age >= 18) when both presence and range are required. CHECK (end_date >= start_date) has the same null behavior. This is not a loophole; it follows SQL's three-valued logic and lets nullability be controlled separately.

sections.title: CHECK at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~custom condition|boolean expression|rejects false rows|business rules in schema
emerald|Examples|~common rules|salary > 0|age >= 18|status IN (...)
amber|NULL behaviour|~unknown passes|NULL satisfies CHECK|add NOT NULL to require|
rose|Gotcha|~MySQL history|ignored before 8.0.16|enforced now|verify your version

sections.title: CHECK constraints in action
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE products (
  id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
  price  DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (price > 0),
  rating INT CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  status VARCHAR(10) CHECK (status IN ('NEW','USED'))
);

INSERT INTO products VALUES (1, 50.00, 4, 'NEW');   -- ok
INSERT INTO products VALUES (2, -5.00, 4, 'NEW');   -- rejected: price > 0 fails
INSERT INTO products VALUES (3, 20.00, 9, 'NEW');   -- rejected: rating out of range
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **App-only validation**: skipping CHECK lets a buggy or second client insert invalid values.
- **Forgetting NULL passes**: a NULL value satisfies CHECK — add `NOT NULL` if a value is required.
- **Assuming old MySQL enforces it**: before 8.0.16 it was ignored.
- **Cross-row logic in CHECK**: CHECK is per-row; it can't reference other rows/tables.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

seo.metaTitle: CHECK Constraint in SQL — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is the CHECK constraint in SQL? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: A products table with a CHECK that keeps price above zero
speakable_v2.hook: CHECK lets the database itself refuse a negative price. But watch the null loophole and the old MySQL that ignored it.

beats.text: A CHECK constraint is your own condition on a column. The database tests it on every insert and update. If the condition comes back false, the write gets rejected. So a business rule like a price above zero lives right in the schema.
App code can validate values too. But a second service or a quick script might skip that check. A CHECK lives in the database, so the rule holds for every writer, every time.

items: It works great for ranges, like a rating between one and five.
It enforces positivity, like a quantity that can't go below zero.
It acts like an enum, with status in a fixed list of values.
Name it for clear errors, like the constraint chk_price.

beats.text: Take a products table where price has a CHECK above zero. Insert a price of minus five and the database rejects it. Here's the non-obvious part. A null price slips through, because a CHECK passes when the condition is unknown. Pair it with NOT NULL when the column needs a value.

items: Leaning on app validation alone, so a stray client writes bad values.
Forgetting that a null value passes a CHECK on its own.
Assuming old MySQL enforces it. Before 8.0.16 it just ignored the rule.
Trying cross-row logic. A CHECK only sees the current row.

speakable_v2.cap: So a CHECK bakes your rules into the table itself. Nulls still slip past, and old MySQL might ignore it.

questions.question: What is the DEFAULT constraint in SQL?
questions.title: DEFAULT Constraint in SQL
questions.direct_answer: A column DEFAULT supplies an expression when an INSERT does not provide that column, or when the DEFAULT keyword is used. Explicit NULL normally remains NULL and can violate NOT NULL; it does not request the default. Defaults can be literals or supported expressions such as CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. They do not retroactively fill existing NULL data unless the ALTER/migration operation does so.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know DEFAULT applies only when the column is omitted, not when NULL is given.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting DEFAULT to replace an explicitly inserted NULL.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention function defaults like CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and pairing DEFAULT with NOT NULL.

sections.title: Column Defaults Apply When a Value Is Omitted
sections.content:
Database defaults are valuable when several writers insert rows and all need the same fallback. An application-side default alone can be bypassed. Generated identity columns and computed/generated columns are related but distinct features.

Changing a default usually affects future inserts only. Plan a separate UPDATE/backfill and constraints when existing rows must change, and verify whether adding a default rewrites/locks a table in the database version used.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Omitted column -> database evaluates its default.
Explicit NULL -> stores NULL if allowed, not the default.
DEFAULT keyword can explicitly request the default in supported statements.
Volatile/expression/default syntax and evaluation timing vary by database.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: CREATE TABLE task (status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW', created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) lets INSERT INTO task (...) omit those columns. INSERT ... status=NULL fails because NOT NULL sees an explicit null. A default is not a validation rule that converts every missing-looking value; an empty string also remains an empty string where the database distinguishes it.

sections.title: DEFAULT at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~fallback value|used when column omitted|keeps rows populated|sensible starting state
emerald|Examples|~common defaults|status = 'ACTIVE'|created_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP|count = 0
amber|Rule|~omit vs NULL|omit column -> default used|explicit NULL -> NULL stored|defaults don't override NULL
rose|Pair with|~NOT NULL|DEFAULT + NOT NULL|fallback always applies|blocks explicit NULL

sections.title: Explicit NULL skips the default
Omit the column (or add NOT NULL) to use the default
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT,
  status VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',  -- NOT NULL forces the fallback
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

INSERT INTO users (id) VALUES (1);
-- status = 'ACTIVE', created_at = now() -> defaults applied
```

Sample row:

| id | status | created_at |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ACTIVE | 2026-06-04 10:00:00 |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting DEFAULT to replace explicit NULL**: it only applies when the column is omitted.
- **No NOT NULL with DEFAULT**: callers can still store NULL explicitly.
- **Static value where a function is needed**: use `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`, not a hard-coded date.
- **Relying on DEFAULT for required business data**: defaults are fallbacks, not validation.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

seo.metaTitle: DEFAULT Constraint in SQL — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is the DEFAULT constraint in SQL? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: A users table with status DEFAULT active and created_at DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
speakable_v2.hook: A DEFAULT fills in for a missing column. But insert null on purpose and it steps aside. It'll keep your null instead.

beats.text: A DEFAULT constraint gives a column a fallback value. The database uses it when an insert leaves that column out. So your rows stay filled in, and you don't repeat every column each time.
Lots of columns have an obvious starting state. A new user is active. A row's created time is right now. A counter starts at zero. A DEFAULT sets that for you, so the insert stays short and clean.

items: Use a literal like a status of active or pending.
Use a function like CURRENT_TIMESTAMP for a created time.
Pair DEFAULT with NOT NULL to force the fallback to win.
Treat a DEFAULT as a starting value, not as real validation.

beats.text: Say status has a DEFAULT of active. Skip the column on insert and the row comes out active. Here's the non-obvious part. Insert null on purpose and the database stores null, not active. The default only fires when you leave the column out entirely.

items: Expecting a DEFAULT to replace an explicit null. It won't.
Skipping NOT NULL, so a caller can still store a null.
Hard-coding a date instead of using CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
Leaning on a DEFAULT for required business data.

speakable_v2.cap: So a DEFAULT covers the missing column. An explicit null still wins, so pair it with NOT NULL when it matters.
followup_handoff: If you INSERT NULL explicitly into a DEFAULT column, what value is stored?
What is DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP used for?

questions.question: What is the NOT NULL constraint in SQL and how is it different from an empty string?
questions.title: NOT NULL Constraint vs Empty String in SQL
questions.direct_answer: NOT NULL rejects the SQL null marker. In most databases an empty character string is a non-null value of length zero, so NOT NULL alone accepts it. Oracle Database is an important exception because it currently treats a zero-length character value as null. Use a CHECK or application rule when non-blank text is required, and verify database-specific trimming and character semantics.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you distinguish NULL (missing) from an empty string (a real, zero-length value).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming NOT NULL also blocks empty strings.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Add a CHECK (length > 0) when you must forbid empty strings, since NOT NULL alone won't.

sections.title: NOT NULL and Empty Strings
sections.content:
Whitespace is another separate value. A string containing one space is neither null nor zero-length in most systems, although CHAR padding and comparison rules can make behavior surprising.

Constraints should express the business rule. If a nickname may be omitted, nullable text can be valid. If a legal name is required, use NOT NULL plus a non-blank check and consistent normalization. Test the actual collation and database rather than relying on a universal empty-string rule.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: NULL means missing/unknown; an empty string usually means known text with no characters.
NOT NULL enforces presence only, not non-blank content.
Oracle treats empty character strings as null.
Use an appropriate CHECK such as length(trim(name)) > 0 when the database supports the intended functions.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: In PostgreSQL or MySQL, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL accepts ''. To reject empty or whitespace-only values, add a database constraint suited to that engine and validate in the application for a friendly message. In Oracle, inserting '' into a character column behaves as null and violates NOT NULL. Therefore 'a NOT NULL column always happily accepts empty string' is not portable SQL advice.

sections.title: NOT NULL vs Empty String
sections.content:
blue|NOT NULL|~must have a value|rejects NULL|enforced on write|required field
emerald|Empty string ''|~known, zero-length|a real value|passes NOT NULL|different from NULL
rose|NULL|~unknown/missing|fails NOT NULL|IS NULL to test|not the same as ''
amber|Forbid empty|~need more|NOT NULL + CHECK(LENGTH>0)|blocks both NULL and ''|

sections.title: NOT NULL alone lets empty strings in
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);

INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (NULL);  -- rejected (NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('');    -- ACCEPTED: '' is a real value
```

sections.title: Add a CHECK to forbid empty strings too
sections.content:
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL CHECK (LENGTH(TRIM(name)) > 0)
);

INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('');     -- rejected by the CHECK
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Ravi'); -- ok
```

*`NOT NULL` blocks missing values; the `CHECK` blocks blank ones.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking NOT NULL blocks `''`**: it doesn't — an empty string is a valid value.
- **Treating NULL like `''` in queries**: `WHERE col = ''` won't find NULLs; use `IS NULL`.
- **Mapping nullable columns to primitives in JPA**: use wrapper types for nullable columns.
- **Forgetting TRIM**: a string of spaces passes a naive `LENGTH > 0` check.

sections.title: How the choices differ
sections.content: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies each row: it's **UNIQUE + NOT NULL**, and a table has **only one**. A **UNIQUE** constraint also prevents duplicates but **allows NULLs** (usually one or more) and you can have **many** per table. Use PRIMARY KEY for identity, UNIQUE for other no-duplicate columns like email.

beats.text: NOT NULL means a column must always hold a value. An empty string's a real value with zero length. So they're not the same thing at all. Null means missing or unknown. An empty string's known and fully present.

Use NOT NULL when a column must always carry some value. That'll block the missing case. But if you also need to forbid blanks, NOT NULL won't do it alone. Add a CHECK on the trimmed length so empty and space-only text gets rejected too.
Declare name as NOT NULL. Insert null and the database rejects it. Insert empty quotes and it'll go straight in. That's the gotcha. To block both, add a CHECK on the trimmed length.
